changes.beforeEn: A character runs forward, stops, and comes back. How much of that motion can we learn from only the starting and finishing positions? We will first record position and time with consistent units, then move from an average over an interval to the rate of change at one instant. Finally, we will combine the slope of a path with travel speed to calculate how quickly the character gains height.
changes.afterEn: In Super Mario Odyssey, Mario crosses a room, follows the wall, and returns toward its middle. Can the starting and finishing positions alone tell us how far he traveled or how his motion changed? We will record position and time with consistent units, move from an interval average to the rate of change at one instant, then combine path slope and travel speed to calculate the rate of gaining height. First, let us decide what to record from the motion we just saw.
changes.reason: Replace unseen forward-stop-reverse placeholder with observed Mario2480–2498. Preserve thesis and full source order; not an exactly closed loop.

changes.beforeEn: If an average hides the motion inside an interval, how can we obtain the velocity right now? At a single instant both changes are zero, so direct substitution gives zero divided by zero. Instead, choose a short interval starting at that instant. A straight position graph has the same slope over every interval. On a curved graph, shortening the interval lets us examine the motion increasingly close to the chosen instant.
changes.afterEn: As a car starts in Forza Horizon 5, its position along the road and the speedometer reading keep changing. The average over the section just traveled and the displayed speed right now answer different questions. If an average hides the motion inside an interval, how can we obtain the velocity right now? At a single instant both changes are zero, so direct substitution gives zero divided by zero. Instead, choose a short interval starting at that instant. A straight position graph has the same slope over every interval. On a curved graph, shortening the interval lets us examine the motion increasingly close to the chosen instant.
changes.reason: Observed speed readout supports motivation for instantaneous rate, without claiming internal derivative algorithm or constant acceleration.

changes.beforeKo: 함수 두 개를 더했다면 각각 미분한 뒤 더할 수 있습니다. 일직선으로 움직이는 기차 안에서 사람이 같은 방향으로 걸어가는 경우를 떠올려 보죠. 지면에서 본 사람의 위치는 기차의 위치와 기차 안에서의 상대 위치를 합한 것입니다. 그래서 지면에서 본 속도도 두 속도의 합이 됩니다. 기차가 초속 십 미터, 사람이 기차 안에서 초속 이 미터로 걸으면 합쳐서 초속 십이 미터예요. 여기서는 기준축이 돌지 않는 일직선 운동으로 비교합니다.

changes.beforeEn: The derivative of a sum equals the sum of the derivatives. Imagine a person walking forward inside a train traveling along a straight line. Relative to the ground, the person’s position is the train’s position plus their position inside the train. Their ground velocity is therefore the sum of the two velocities: ten meters per second for the train plus two inside it gives twelve. Here we use aligned, nonrotating axes along a straight track.
changes.afterEn: In Tears of the Kingdom, Link stands beside the raft’s mast while the riverbank passes by. He is nearly still relative to the raft but moving relative to the shore. The reference used to record position matters. The derivative of a sum equals the sum of the derivatives. Imagine a person walking forward inside a train traveling along a straight line. Relative to the ground, the person’s position is the train’s position plus their position inside the train. Their ground velocity is therefore the sum of the two velocities: ten meters per second for the train plus two inside it gives twelve. Here we use aligned, nonrotating axes along a straight track.
changes.reason: Observed raft-frame relation motivates original straight train/walking example; do not claim Link walks or camera/world axes fixed.

changes.beforeEn: If a function is multiplied by a constant, its derivative is multiplied by the same constant. Converting a position from furlongs to meters multiplies it by two hundred one point one six eight. The derived velocity gets the same conversion factor. Preserving sums and constant multiples is called linearity. It lets us differentiate a polynomial one term at a time and then add the results.
